Start with the thing you already do and never had to justify.

You take a matrix, you take a vector, you dot rows against it, you get a new vector. It works, but it looks like a convention — a rule someone chose. My aim over the next while is to make that rule *inevitable*, and the way in is to be exact about what a vector actually is.

A vector in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is two things at once: a list of two numbers, and an arrow from the origin. The two readings stay in step because both operations behave the same way in each:

$$\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad 2\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$$

Componentwise, and geometrically: tip-to-tail for addition, stretching for scaling. Nothing subtle there.

Now the piece that matters. There are two special arrows — one step east, one step north:

$$\mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

Every vector is a **recipe out of those two**:

$$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = x\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + y\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

Read it plainly: "$x$ steps east, then $y$ steps north, and you're there." The coordinates of a vector aren't a label attached to it — they *are* its recipe in terms of the axes. This is trivial, and it is the lever the entire subject turns on, so I want to be sure your picture of it is exact.

arguments.explanation:
Exactly one, and the weights are just the entries: $(x,y) = x\mathbf{e}_1 + y\mathbf{e}_2$ forces the coefficients, because the first coordinate of $a\mathbf{e}_1 + b\mathbf{e}_2$ is $a$ and the second is $b$. Uniqueness is what makes coordinates mean anything — a vector is not "reachable many ways," it has one recipe along the axes.

Note the second option: perpendicularity is *not* what gives uniqueness. Any two non-parallel directions give unique weights; $(1,2)$ and $(3,1)$ work exactly as well as the axes, just with messier coefficients. Being perpendicular is a convenience, and treating it as a requirement is a habit worth dropping now — it will cost you later in the span and independence material.

The third option confuses "a mix of the axes" with "a mix of anything." And the fourth is false: the axes reach every point, since $x$ and $y$ can be any reals.

That's the miss, and it's worth having caught it this early. Uniqueness has nothing to do with perpendicularity.

Take $\mathbf{u} = (1,2)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (3,1)$ — visibly not perpendicular. Can $(4,3)$ be written as a mix of them? Writing $a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{v} = (4,3)$ gives two equations:

$$a + 3b = 4, \qquad 2a + b = 3$$

From the second, $b = 3-2a$; substituting, $a + 9 - 6a = 4$, so $a = 1$ and $b = 1$. Check: $(1,2) + (3,1) = (4,3)$. One recipe, no perpendicularity anywhere in the arithmetic. What made it one is that the two equations are *independent* — the coefficient matrix has determinant $1\cdot 1 - 3\cdot 2 = -5 \neq 0$. A nonzero determinant says exactly one thing: the two directions are not parallel.

Here's the picture to replace the one you're carrying. The axes give a **square grid**, and the coordinates $(x,y)$ say which grid corner you're at. Two non-parallel directions give a **slanted grid of parallelograms** — different shapes, identical logic: every point of the plane sits at exactly one corner. Slant doesn't break the coordinate system. Perpendicularity only makes the parallelograms into rectangles.

And the one-line proof, so this isn't an assertion you're taking on faith. Suppose $a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{v} = a'\mathbf{u} + b'\mathbf{v}$. Rearranging, $(a-a')\mathbf{u} = (b'-b)\mathbf{v}$: the left side lies along $\mathbf{u}$, the right side along $\mathbf{v}$. If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ aren't parallel, the only way those can be the same vector is both being zero — so $a = a'$ and $b = b'$. Non-parallel is what does the work.

The failure case, for contrast: let $\mathbf{v} = 2\mathbf{u}$. Then everything you can reach is $(a + 2b)\mathbf{u}$, a single line, and each point on it has infinitely many recipes. A point off that line has none.

I'm having an interactive one built for this — two draggable directions, a live slanted grid, and a target point with its recipe solved out — it should land in a minute, and it's the fastest way to make your eye stop demanding right angles.

Which brings us to the thing we've been avoiding. A matrix is four numbers. Yet it supposedly *does* something to the plane. What kind of action can be captured by a fixed, finite table of numbers?

Look at what you can do to the plane: rotate it, stretch it, shear it on a slanted grid, flatten it onto a line, reflect it. You cannot compress it non-uniformly, fold it, or bend it — a table of four numbers simply cannot record that much. So the maps we get to study are exactly the ones that **don't bend the grid**: straight lines stay straight, parallel stays parallel, evenly spaced stays evenly spaced, and the origin stays where it is.

That property has a name, and it is the only definition in this whole arc that I'm going to hand you flat:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> A map $L$ is **linear** if it respects the two vector operations:
> $$L(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = L(\mathbf{u}) + L(\mathbf{v}), \qquad L(c\mathbf{u}) = c\,L(\mathbf{u})$$

Add then map, or map then add — same answer. Scale then map, or map then scale — same answer. That's the whole requirement.

Rotation passes both tests: rotating $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ gives the same arrow as rotating each and then adding (the parallelogram rotates rigidly), and rotating $2\mathbf{u}$ gives twice the rotated arrow. Lengths and angles are preserved, so nothing is bent.

- Reflecting across $y = x+1$ also moves the origin (to $(-1,1)$), so it fails for the same reason, even though reflection itself is a linear idea when the line runs through the origin.

CANVAS: a 2D plane centered at the origin, dark background, clean light square reference grid (spacing 1 unit), labeled axes, high-contrast sans-serif. Single self-contained HTML file, no external libraries.

CONTROLS: four sliders for the entries of A = [[a, b], [c, d]], each ranging -2 to 2 in steps of 0.1, defaults a=1, b=1, c=0, d=1 (a shear). Show the matrix numerically, arranged in its 2x2 grid layout, updating live.

VISUALS (all updating live and continuously while dragging a slider):
1. The standard integer grid (all lines x = integer and y = integer) drawn transformed by A, in a faint color — so the whole plane visibly deforms.
2. The unit square in the original plane drawn as a dashed ghost outline, and its image — the parallelogram spanned by the two columns — filled with a translucent color and outlined solid.
3. The images of the basis vectors as bold arrows from the origin: e1 -> first column (distinct color, labeled "col 1 = A e1"), e2 -> second column (another color, labeled "col 2 = A e2"). Show the original e1 and e2 as faint dashed arrows for comparison.
4. A draggable probe vector x, default (1.5, 0.5), drawn as a solid amber arrow from the origin. Its image Ax drawn as a bold arrow in a contrasting color. Also draw the parallelogram decomposition: the segment from the origin to x*col1, then from there to x*col1 + y*col2 = Ax, so the learner sees Ax as a weighted sum of the two columns.
5. Readout strip: det = a*d - b*c to two decimals, with status text: if |det| > 0.02 show "area scaled by |det|"; if det < 0 also show "orientation flipped"; if |det| <= 0.02 show "collapsed onto a line (det = 0) - the columns are parallel" in a warning color.

PRESET BUTTONS that tween the four sliders over ~0.5s: "shear" [[1,1],[0,1]], "rotate 90" [[0,-1],[1,0]], "project onto x-axis" [[1,0],[0,0]], "scale 2" [[2,0],[0,2]], "reflect across y=x" [[0,1],[1,0]], "collapse" [[1,2],[2,4]] (det = 0).

REQUIREMENT: dragging any slider must never break the drawing; clamp to canvas; keep labels legible at all settings. The point that must be unmistakable within ten seconds of dragging: the two columns ARE the images of the axes, and the parallelogram is where the unit square went.

Use it now. Drag the four sliders and watch the whole grid deform — that deformation *is* the matrix, not a picture of it. Then drag the amber probe vector $\mathbf{x}$ around: the dashed segment along $\text{col}_1$ followed by the segment along $\text{col}_2$ lands exactly on $A\mathbf{x}$, so you can see the weighted sum with your eyes. You now have the pivot of the whole subject: a matrix is a record of where the axes land, and multiplying it by a vector means taking that linear combination of its columns. Everything remaining is either a consequence or an application.

Here's the first consequence, and it starts from a gap. You know what one matrix does. What happens with two? In numpy you'd write `B @ A` and get something — but what operation on *transformations* is that product actually performing, and why is it multiplication rather than adding or multiplying entries?

You may assume nothing beyond what's established. To build the combined map — shear by $A$, then rotate by $B$ — the tool you have is: a matrix is determined by where the axes land.

arguments.explanation:
Track the axes through both steps. The combined map sends each basis vector on a journey: first $A$ moves it, then $B$ moves it again. So the combined first column is $B(A\mathbf{e}_1) = B(\text{col}_1$ of $A)$, and the second is $B(\text{col}_2$ of $A)$. Those two vectors, written side by side, ARE the matrix of the composition.

That is matrix multiplication: $(BA)_{kj}$ = row $k$ of $B$ dotted with column $j$ of $A$, because that is what $B(\text{col}_j$ of $A)$ computes. The product is not a definition someone picked — it is forced by "columns are where the axes land."

Order matters, because the two actions don't commute: shearing then rotating is visibly different from rotating then shearing. Elementwise products and entrywise sums have nothing to do with transformations composed in sequence.

Correct, and now make it concrete so the 50% firms up. Take

$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \text{ (shear)}, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \text{ (quarter turn)}$$

and ask for the map "shear, then rotate." Use the tool: track the axes through both steps.

- $\mathbf{e}_1$: $A$ sends it to $(1,0)$ — the shear leaves the horizontal axis alone. Then $B$ sends $(1,0)$ to $(0,1)$. So the combined first column is $(0,1)$.
- $\mathbf{e}_2$: $A$ sends it to $(1,1)$ — the shear tilts it right. Then $B$ sends $(1,1) = 1\cdot(0,1) + 1\cdot(-1,0)$ to $(-1,1)$. So the combined second column is $(-1,1)$.

$$BA = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

Now do it the other way round — rotate first, then shear — and the axes tell a different story. $\mathbf{e}_1 \mapsto (0,1) \mapsto (1,1)$; $\mathbf{e}_2 \mapsto (-1,0) \mapsto (-1,0)$, giving

$$AB = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$$

Different matrix. Composition is not commutative, and now you can say *why* rather than remembering it: the columns record one path through the two maps, and paths don't commute.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Matrix multiplication is composition. $(BA)$'s $j$-th column is $B$ applied to the $j$-th column of $A$ — which is exactly why the entry $(BA)_{kj}$ is row $k$ of $B$ dotted with column $j$ of $A$.

Every weird feature of matrix multiplication — the non-commutativity, the "rows times columns" ritual, the fact that $AB = 0$ is possible with neither factor zero — is a fact about composing transformations. None of it is decoration.

- $\mathbf{e}_1 \xrightarrow{A} (0,1) \xrightarrow{B} (0,1)$ — the stretch leaves vertical alone, so the first column is $(0,1)$.
- $\mathbf{e}_2 \xrightarrow{A} (-1,0) \xrightarrow{B} (-2,0)$ — the stretch doubles the horizontal, so the second column is $(-2,0)$.

So $BA = \begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

The second option is the other order — stretch first, then rotate: $\mathbf{e}_1 \xrightarrow{B} (2,0) \xrightarrow{A} (0,2)$, giving $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\2&0\end{pmatrix}$. Both are legitimate matrices, which is precisely why the order has to be tracked rather than assumed.

So the question that runs underneath everything from here: **given a pile of vectors, what can they actually build, and when does a new vector add something genuinely new?** You have partial footing on this (you saw the redundant system immediately) and one working misconception about it (the perpendicularity habit).

arguments.explanation: Only the plane $z = 0$. Every combination $a\\mathbf{v}_1 + b\\mathbf{v}_2 + c\\mathbf{v}_3$ has third entry $0\\cdot a + 0\\cdot b + 0\\cdot c = 0$, so the third coordinate can never move off zero. Right, and the correction to make now is the one that kills counting as a strategy: the number of vectors says nothing about how much they build. What matters is how many genuinely *distinct directions* are among them.

Three definitions, and they're short:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> - The **span** of a set of vectors is everything you can build from it — all linear combinations. In the plane that's a point, a line, or the whole plane; in $\mathbb{R}^3$ a point, a line, a plane, or all of space. Always through the origin.
> - A set is **linearly independent** if no vector in it can be built from the others — every vector contributes a direction the rest can't supply. Otherwise it's **dependent**, and the extra vectors are pure redundancy.
> - A **basis** is independent *and* spanning: exactly enough vectors, no waste and no gaps.

Three things worth noticing immediately.

**A span is made of sums, not unions.** The span of two non-parallel directions is the entire plane, including points that lie on neither line — that's what adding lets you reach.

**Dependence has a crisp test.** A set is dependent exactly when some non-trivial combination of it gives $\mathbf{0}$. In your $\mathbb{R}^3$ case, $\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2 - \mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{0}$, so the third was never new.

**A basis is what makes coordinates possible** — and it's any basis, not just the axes. If a set is a basis, every point has exactly one recipe as a combination of it; that's the uniqueness result you proved earlier for the axes, and it holds for any independent spanning set, slanted or not. Coordinates aren't intrinsic to a point; they're a description relative to a chosen basis. That distinction is the whole reason a change of basis is a move you can make at all.

That collision is the whole story of rank, and it has a name: the **kernel**, or null space — the set of inputs the map destroys. For a linear map it's never a random scatter of vectors; it's always a subspace through the origin (if $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ and $A\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}$ then $A(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{0}$ too, so kernels are closed under combination just like spans).

Here's the structure that falls out, and it's worth writing down as a single block because these are the same fact in five costumes:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with columns $\text{col}_1,\dots,\text{col}_n$:
> - Every output is a combination of the columns, so the set of reachable outputs is exactly $\text{span}(\text{col}_1,\dots,\text{col}_n)$ — the **column space**.
> - **Rank** = the number of independent columns = the dimension of the column space = how many dimensions of output the map actually reaches.
> - $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is solvable **iff** $\mathbf{b}$ lies in the column space. Nothing else governs it.
> - **Rank–nullity:** $\text{rank} + \dim(\ker A) = n$. Dimensions reached plus dimensions destroyed equals dimensions of input — a conservation law.
> - $A$ is invertible **iff** rank $= n$ **iff** $\ker A = \{\mathbf{0}\}$ **iff** $\det A \neq 0$.

Two consequences to make concrete. First, why collisions are structured: if $A\mathbf{x} = A\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{b}$, then $A(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}') = \mathbf{0}$, so the solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ are exactly *one* solution plus the whole kernel. That's one particular solution, plus a line (or plane) of sliding freedom. Second, what inversion means: $A^{-1}$ exists exactly when nothing is lost, which is exactly when the kernel is trivial — and that is what people are really testing when they compute a determinant.

Right, and the reasoning you gave is the perpendicular case working backwards — which is exactly the fact I want to derive rather than assert.

**Why is $\sum_i u_iv_i$ the alignment measure?**

Start from the one pairing that suggests itself: to combine two lists of numbers into a single number, multiply slot-by-slot and add. That gives $x_1y_1 + x_2y_2$. The question is whether it measures anything geometric.

Here's the discovery. Three vectors form a triangle: $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$, and the arrow $\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$ closing the gap between their tips. Two facts about that triangle:

*Geometry* — the law of cosines, applied to the side $\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}$ opposite the angle $\theta$ between $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$:

$$\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{u}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 - 2\|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta$$

*Coordinates* — the same quantity, computed by expanding:

$$\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|^2 = (x_1-y_1)^2 + (x_2-y_2)^2 = (x_1^2 + x_2^2) + (y_1^2 + y_2^2) - 2(x_1y_1 + x_2y_2)$$

Since $x_1^2+x_2^2 = \|\mathbf{u}\|^2$ and $y_1^2+y_2^2 = \|\mathbf{v}\|^2$, the two computations already agree on the first two terms. They describe the same length, so the leftovers must agree too:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> $$\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 = \|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta$$

So the sum-of-products isn't a convention either — it's forced by the geometry of a triangle, and it's the only arithmetic that could report the angle. Three consequences worth carrying:

- **Perpendicularity is the zero case.** $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0 \iff$ one length is zero or $\cos\theta = 0$. Which is why orthogonality is expressed as an equation rather than a picture.
- **Length comes out of the dot product free.** $\|\mathbf{u}\| = \sqrt{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}}$, since $\cos 0 = 1$.
- **The sign carries information.** Positive means the vectors lean the same way, negative means opposed, and the magnitude on top of that reports how strongly.

One last thing, which matters more in ML than in geometry: in two or three dimensions you can *see* the angle. In 768-dimensional embedding space you cannot — there's no picture available. There, $\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|}$ is not a shortcut to the angle; it is the only definition of angle you have. Which is why cosine similarity is the standard similarity measure in that setting, and why raw dot products have to be normalized before comparison.

Pair B: $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 2$, $\|\mathbf{u}\| = 1$, $\|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{2^2 + 0.5^2} = \sqrt{4.25} \approx 2.062$, so $\cos\theta \approx 0.970$ — about $14^\circ$.

$$\text{proj}_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{v} = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}}\,\mathbf{u}, \qquad \text{remainder} = \mathbf{v} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{v}$$

Here they are, cleanly, and together in one place — these three ideas are one idea seen from three angles.

**Kernel** (null space) of $A$: all vectors it sends to zero.

$$\ker A = \{\mathbf{x} : A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\}$$

It always contains $\mathbf{0}$, and it's always a subspace. Its dimension is how many directions of input the map destroys.

**Singular**: a square matrix whose kernel is bigger than $\{\mathbf{0}\}$ — one that destroys at least one direction of input. Equivalently, rank $< n$.

**Non-singular** = invertible. Nothing destroyed, kernel is just $\{\mathbf{0}\}$, rank $= n$, and $\det \neq 0$.

The determinant earns its role here: $\det A$ is the factor by which $A$ scales area (or volume, in higher dimensions). If $A$ collapses a direction, it collapses all area with it, so $\det A = 0$ exactly when a direction is lost. That's why the same condition keeps appearing.

| Statement | Equivalent to |
|---|---|
| $\ker A \neq \{\mathbf{0}\}$ | some nonzero $\mathbf{x}$ has $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ |
| rank $< n$ | the columns are linearly dependent |
| $\det A = 0$ | $A$ squashes at least one dimension away |
| $A$ is singular | $A^{-1}$ does not exist |
| $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has infinitely many solutions (when solvable) | one particular solution + the kernel |

Now the reason this vocabulary was needed at exactly that moment: it is what turns "find the directions that survive" into an equation you can solve. $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$ is a statement that $A - \lambda I$ is singular — and singular means $\det = 0$, which is solvable for $\lambda$.

Right, and your reasoning is the correct one — the small eigenvalue attenuates its own component so thoroughly that the other component comes to dominate the direction. Now the algebra that makes it precise.

Powers of $A$ come free from the decomposition, because the coordinate changes cancel in the middle:

$$A^2 = (PDP^{-1})(PDP^{-1}) = PD(P^{-1}P)DP^{-1} = PD^2P^{-1}$$

and by induction:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> $$A^n = P D^n P^{-1}, \qquad D^n = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1^n & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & \lambda_n^n\end{pmatrix}$$

Repeated application in the eigenbasis is nothing but independent scaling of each coefficient. Write $\mathbf{x} = a\mathbf{p}_1 + b\mathbf{p}_2$; after $n$ steps the coefficients are $\lambda_1^n a$ and $\lambda_2^n b$, each racing on its own growth factor with no interaction.

Everything about repeated maps follows:

- $|\lambda| > 1$ **grows**, $|\lambda| < 1$ **decays**, and since $D^n$ takes powers, these compound.
- A **negative** eigenvalue flips sign each step — the vector alternates sides of the origin — but its *magnitude* still grows or shrinks by $|\lambda|^n$.
- The largest $|\lambda|$ **dominates**, because the ratio $(\lambda_1/\lambda_2)^n$ explodes. Given enough steps, $A^n\mathbf{x}$ points along the dominant eigenvector regardless of where it started.

That last fact is an algorithm. **Power iteration**: to find the top eigenvector of a matrix too large to factor, pick a vector at random, multiply by $A$ a few hundred times, and read off the direction. It converges for the reason above. This is how PageRank was computed, and it's how PCA is done on data too big to form the covariance matrix explicitly.

And it clarifies what an eigenvalue means in the ML setting: the dominant eigen-direction is the direction the matrix **amplifies most**. For a covariance matrix, amplifying a direction means that direction carries the most variance. Same statement, two vocabularies.

That edge case is worth remembering as the boundary of "the dominant direction wins": it wins because everything else is present and getting out-competed, not because it pulls from nothing.

Now the payoff node, where all three branches meet. **PCA**, the standard tool for reducing a dataset's dimension.

Set the scene in ML terms. Your data is a matrix $X$: one row per sample, one column per feature. In 2D, picture a cloud of points — mostly elongated along some diagonal, since real features correlate. Compression means replacing each point by a couple of numbers along well-chosen directions, and projecting onto those directions. Choose the directions badly and your compressed data tells you almost nothing about the original cloud.

So which directions would you choose?

arguments.explanation: The directions in which the data spreads out most. The logic: after you project, what survives is how far apart the points are along your chosen directions. A direction where every point sits near the same value carries almost no information — all points would land on nearly the same number, so the compression would be lossy in the extreme. A direction of wide spread keeps the points distinguishable, so most of the structure is retained.\n\nEquivalently and more precisely: you want the projection that loses the least squared distance between points. That is a *minimum-error* criterion, and its solution is the maximum-variance directions — the same choice seen from two sides. The last option, the mean of the data, is a single point and therefore not a direction at all; the second is just a convention, and for correlated data the axes are usually the worst possible choice.
